justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 303.5 for the one-day forecast and gradually rising to 308.0 at the one-month horizon. The one-day estimate was anchored primarily to recent price action and short-term momentum, assuming no major catalysts would materially disrupt the prevailing trend overnight. The one-week estimate edged slightly higher to account for a mild continuation of whatever underlying trend was in place, while the one-month estimate incorporated a slightly more optimistic drift assumption consistent with longer-run mean reversion toward fair value or trend-following dynamics. In all three cases, the point estimates represent my best central guess under relatively benign, status-quo conditions.

The confidence interval widths expand significantly as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 17 points, reflecting normal daily volatility and the possibility of modest surprise moves from scheduled data releases or news flow. At one week, the interval widens to 34 points, incorporating the possibility of multiple compounding daily moves, sentiment shifts, or macro developments. At one month, the interval stretches to 66 points, acknowledging that over a four-week window, a meaningful shift in the fundamental or macro backdrop — interest rate expectations, earnings surprises, geopolitical developments — could substantially alter the trajectory.

Several specific risks could push realized outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data, a hawkish policy surprise from a central bank, or a sudden escalation in geopolitical tensions could drive prices well below the lower bounds of my intervals, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons. Liquidity disruptions or a broader risk-off episode in financial markets could amplify such moves. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst — such as a better-than-expected earnings season, a dovish policy pivot, or a resolution of a key geopolitical risk — could propel prices above the upper bounds, especially over the one-month window where more events have time to materialize.

It is also worth noting that my intervals, while wide, are not exhaustive of all possible outcomes. Tail events — flash crashes, systemic shocks, or completely unanticipated news — by definition sit outside a 90% confidence interval, meaning there is still a 10% probability mass in the tails. My forecasts should be treated as probabilistic guidance rather than precise predictions, and decision-makers should stress-test against scenarios well outside these ranges when stakes are high.
